title: A morning word
hookLine: a line from a text you love
tomorrow: a man moves to a new city for love. does his journey count?

lines: ONE QUOTE FOR YEARS, OR A NEW ONE DAILY?
cards: Some people keep one quote on the lock screen for years. Others want a fresh verse of the day every morning. Desert monks wrestled with something close to this.

John Cassian tells how he and his friend Germanus traveled to Egypt to learn from the desert elders, and asked one of them, Abba Isaac, a question they couldn't let go of: how do you pray without ceasing, when the mind won't sit still for a minute?
His answer was a single line.

teach.b: The line is from a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me." Isaac's case: say it on waking, at work, when you're tempted, when you're glad.
One short verse fits every mood, so the mind always has a place to come home to. That's one view: one line, kept for life. The other view lives in the same monasteries.

teach.h: OR LECTIO: READ ON, DAY BY DAY.
teach.b: Benedict's Rule sets hours every day for lectio, slow reading, and the monk reads on, so the reading keeps moving through new pages. Let both speak.
For the daily reading: a single line can wear smooth and go dead in the mouth, and a new page keeps surprising you.
For the one verse: a new line every day can turn into browsing, and the one line goes deep because it never changes.
The monasteries kept both. Benedict's monks open their hours of prayer with Isaac's very verse, and then they read on, page by page. Here is the teaching under it.

teach.h: A WORD CARRIED, NOT ONLY READ.
teach.b: In the Christian monastic tradition, a word of scripture is meant to be carried, not only read: repeated until it sinks in, so the day is lived inside it.
On your own path the question is which you need right now: a line to come home to, or a line to wake you up.

how: Monks and nuns who follow Benedict's Rule begin the hours of prayer with the verse 'O God, come to my assistance', and keep set times for lectio, the slow reading of scripture.

o: a quote your phone shows you every morning
the first thing you say aloud to someone after waking
one line you carry from your reading into the day

games.q: the desert and the monastery: tap the pairs.
p: the two monks who asked him
slow reading of scripture, day by day
O God, come to my assistance

s: Abba Isaac told the monks to read a new psalm every morning
he gave them one verse to keep saying, in every mood, all day.
Benedict's monks open their hours of prayer with the verse Isaac taught
the Rule opens the hours of the day with 'O God, come to my assistance'.
the monks had to choose one method and give up the other
the monasteries kept both: the one verse and the daily reading.

games.q: your friend reads one new verse every morning. her brother says that's just browsing. what's the best case for her side?
o: a new passage, read slowly, keeps the word fresh; Benedict's monks read on daily.
Isaac's verse is too old to fit a modern life, so anything new is better.
the more lines you collect, the faster the habit counts as real prayer.
games.why: lectio is the other half of the monastic day: slow reading, page after page. the monasteries kept it beside Isaac's one verse.

practice: Choose a line you could carry: Isaac's verse, a line of a poem, a sentence from a text you love. Say it out loud, slowly, three times, and notice which word lands heaviest.
If it still sounds true the third time, write it under tomorrow's first minute in your notebook.

wordCard.voice: A morning word: one line you carry into the day. For Abba Isaac, a single psalm verse; for Benedict's readers, the next page.

orig.note: Latin: the opening of Isaac's psalm verse, as Benedict's monks begin each hour.

carryVoice: Keep this close: my morning line, a word carried, not only read. Back again tomorrow.
